activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
fact: Dress-up clothes help you pretend to be someone else.
story:
Jaxon walked in the forest with Ms. Ricci. He saw a box under a big tree. The box had a hat, a scarf, and some shiny boots. "Who wears this?" he asked. "You can wear it," said Ms. Ricci. Jaxon put on the big hat. He stood very tall. "Now I am a firefighter!" he said. "The dress-up clothes make me someone new."

His friends Shepherd and Judith came down the path. "Look, look!" said Jaxon. "I am a firefighter!" Judith put on the scarf. "Now I am a mama," she said. Shepherd put on the boots. "I am a farmer now," he said. They all laughed.

The farmer had a carrot. "My baby bunny is hungry," said the mama. The firefighter helped. "I will bring the carrot fast!" said Jaxon. He ran, but not too fast, and gave the carrot to the soft toy bunny. The bunny was not hungry anymore. "Is the bunny okay now?" asked Jaxon. "Yes, all better," said Judith.

Then the pretend phone rang. Beep, beep! "Come quick!" said Shepherd. "A little cat is stuck!" The firefighter put on his big hat again. He held his toy hose. He sprayed pretend water on a pretend fire. The cat was saved. The mama hugged the cat. The farmer clapped. Jaxon took off the big hat at the end of the day. He was just Jaxon again. But he smiled all the way home. "Can we play again soon?" he asked Ms. Ricci. "Yes," she said. "Tomorrow we play again."

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: If you get lost in a store, tell a store worker you can't find your grown-up.
story:
Carter went to the playground with his mom. First he went down the slide. Then he ran in the green grass. "One slide, two swings, three big steps," he counted. His mom waved from a bench.

After play time, they walked to the little store next to the playground. Mom said, "Stay close." Carter saw apples. He saw a big tower of cans. Then he looked up. Mom was not there. The tall shelf had hidden her.

Carter remembered what his dad had taught him. He walked to the front. The cashier had curly hair. "I can't find my grown-up," Carter said. The cashier called out, and Mom came running around the shelf. "You told a store worker," Mom said. "That was just right."

Then a small surprise came. Azalea from his class popped out from behind the juice boxes. "Carter! We play at my house next door," she said. Carter counted again: "One apple, two friends, three happy people." Mom held his hand all the way to the door.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: When people feel sad, they sometimes cry.
story:
Luke had a toy snake at school. It was green and long. He loved that snake.

At play time, Luke saw Liana. She sat by the wooden blocks. Tears ran down her face. She was crying. Luke felt sad too.

He ran to his cubby. He got his toy snake. He held it out to Liana. "You can hold him," Luke said. Liana wiped her eyes. She took the soft snake. She hugged it close.

Then Liana smiled a big smile. "His name is Sam," she said. Luke sat down next to her. They made a little home for Sam out of blocks. Mr. Lin came over and helped them cover the snake with a small blanket.

"More blocks," said Liana. She handed one to Luke.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: Shirts, socks and hats are all clothes.
story:
Emmett hurried to the dress-up corner at school. He wanted to wear the firefighter hat. But his shoe felt funny. One sock was gone!

"Where is my sock?" Emmett asked. He looked under the chair. No sock. He looked in the short basket of hats. No sock. He looked in the toy box. Yes! His sock was lying on top of a teddy bear.

Emmett picked up the sock. He laughed. "A sock is not a toy," he said. "It goes with clothes. Shirts, socks and hats are all clothes."

Yousuf came over. He was holding his shirt. "My shirt fell in the toy box too," Yousuf said.

"Then we can fix it," Emmett said. He put his sock in the clothes basket. He counted out loud, "One sock, one shirt, one hat." Yousuf added his shirt. "Now two shirts!" he said.

Ms. Munro smiled. "You made the corner neat," she said. "Thank you, boys."

Emmett put on his sock and shoe. Then he put on the firefighter hat. He looked out the window at the big tree. "Firefighter to the rescue!" he said.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
fact: Mixing yellow paint and blue paint makes green.
story:
Theodore sat at the paint table at summer camp. He wanted to paint the long grass by the lake. But there was no green paint in his tray. He had red, yellow, and blue. He looked and looked. Still no green.

His friend Khaled sat down next to him. "I need green for the grass," Theodore said. "I only have yellow and blue." Khaled pointed at the jars. "Yellow is a sun colour," he said. "Blue is a sky colour."

Theodore dipped his brush in the yellow paint. He painted a big yellow stripe on his paper. Then he dipped the same brush in the blue paint. He made a blue stripe right on top. He swirled his brush round and round. The colours touched. The wet paint moved together.

The stripe turned green! Theodore jumped up. "Khaled, look! It's green!" He painted long green grass all the way across his paper. He even gave the stick figure in his picture green shoes. Ms. Pérez came over and smiled. "What lovely grass, Theodore." Theodore held up his wet painting so she could see. "It's yellow and blue," he said.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
fact: Setting the cup down on the table before pouring keeps it still.
story:
Riley stood in the restaurant kitchen. The cook had made hot toast, and it sat on a plate. "Now you can butter it," the cook said. Riley took the knife and scooped soft butter. She spread it slow, corner to corner. "Look, shiny toast!" she said. Mr. Kaminski smiled. "Nice work, Riley."

Next came the milk. Riley held a cup in one hand. She poured with the other hand. The cup wiggled. Milk plopped onto the table. "Sorry, milk," Riley said. Mr. Kaminski handed her a cloth. Riley wiped it up.

Then she set the cup down on the table. She let go of it. The cup sat still. Riley poured, and the milk went right in. Not one drop spilled. Riley hopped up and down. "The cup stays still when I put it down!" Jolene clapped from the door. "Can I try too?"

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: When you are scared, you can tell a grown-up you trust, and they can help.
story:
Leah was almost asleep. Then she heard a sound. Tap. Tap. Tap. It came from under her bed. Leah sat up fast. Her heart went boom, boom. She was scared. She pulled the blanket up high. The sound came again. Tap. Tap. Tap. Leah did not like it one bit.

She thought for a minute. She was a young girl, but she knew something good. When you are scared, you can tell a grown-up you trust, and they can help. So she called out, "Mom! I hear a sound!" Mom came in fast. She sat on the bed. "I'm scared," Leah said. "It goes tap, tap, tap." Mom held her hand. Leah pointed one finger down at the floor. "It's under there," she said.

Mom got down on her knees. She looked under the bed. Then she laughed a little laugh. Out came the cat! He had been batting a toy. Tap. Tap. Tap. That was his little game all along. The cat jumped up on the bed. He curled up by Leah's feet. His tail was soft and warm.

Leah was not scared anymore. She felt happy and sleepy too. Mom kissed her head. "Call me any time," Mom said. "I will always come." Leah closed her eyes. The cat purred by her toes. It sounded like a tiny motor. Tap. Tap. Tap, said the toy on the floor. The cat did not care. He was already asleep.

"Good night, cat," Leah whispered.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: A tiny new plant poking up out of the soil is called a sprout.
story:
Isla went to the garden center with her dad. She picked a small bag of seeds. "Carrot seeds," she said. She held the bag like a little ball all the way home.

In the yard, Isla dug in the dirt. She made the soil clean and soft. Her dad helped her break up the big lumps. Isla patted the seeds down into the dirt. Then she gave them a drink of water.

Every day Isla ran outside to look. She saw only brown dirt. She saw a worm. She saw a leaf blow by. But no carrots came up. "Too slow," said Isla. Her dad laughed. "Wait more days," he said.

At last, Isla saw something tiny and green. It was poking up out of the soil. She ran to the fence. "Hector! Come see my sprout!" she called. Hector ran over fast. "A sprout?" he said. "Yes," said Isla. She pointed at the little green tip. "That is a sprout. My seeds made it." Hector bent down low. "It is so small," he said. "It will grow big," said Isla. She gave the sprout one more drop of water.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
fact: On a windy day, you can see trees sway and leaves blow around.
story:
David sat in his car seat. He looked out the window. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. David wore his sunglasses.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain fell on the window. Tap, tap, tap. "Rainy now," said David. His dad turned on the wipers. The rain went away, swish, swish.

"Where is my hat?" David asked. "We might need it." His dad said, "Look at the trees."

The trees swayed back and forth. Leaves blew all around. They blew across the road. They blew past the car. "It is windy!" said David. He counted the leaves as they flew. One, two, three. The wind took them far away.

"Wind makes the trees dance," said David. His dad smiled. The last leaf flew up, up, up. Then it landed on a big hill.

"The hill is white," said David. "Snow!" His dad said, "Yes. We will need warm coats."

David hugged his hat. "I am ready," he said.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
fact: A rectangle has four sides and four square corners, like the shape of a door.
story:
Adam wanted to draw a farm picture. He had paper and crayons. But he needed a shape for the barn door. "I need the door shape," he said. "But which one is it?"

Mom was cooking at the stove. Adam stayed back from the hot stove. He looked around the sunny kitchen. He saw a plate. "That is a circle," he said. He saw a window. "That is a square." He saw a slice of toast. "That is a triangle!" But no door shape yet.

Then Adam looked at the big kitchen door. He ran to it. He touched one side. Then another side. "One, two, three, four sides!" He poked each corner. "One, two, three, four corners. And they are square corners!" The dog barked, as if to say yes. "A rectangle has four sides and four square corners," said Adam, "like the shape of a door!"

Adam ran back to the table. He drew four sides and four square corners. He drew a red barn around it. He drew a sunny sky and a cow. "The farm is done!" he shouted. Mom clapped her hands. The dog barked again, loud and happy.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: A library puts its books on shelves in groups so people can find them.
story:
Penelope sat at the dinner table. Her plate had peas, cheese and bread. Under her chair, her boot tapped the floor. One boot was on. One boot was lost somewhere.

"I want a book about animals," said Penelope. "The cat book. With the big tiger."

"We can go to the library tomorrow," said her dad. "The animal books sit together on one shelf. The toy books sit on another shelf."

Penelope looked at her plate. She had an idea. The dinner table could be a library!

She pushed all her peas into one group. "These are the animal peas," she said. She pushed her bread into another group. "These are the toy breads." The cheese got its own spot too. "Food books," she said, and giggled.

Then she dropped some cheese, and it went splat. "The cheese is glue now," she said. "It sticks my groups down."

Her dad laughed and helped wipe the table. "Now the table is clean again," he said.

The next day they went to the library. Penelope held her dad's hand. She found a big shelf full of animal books. Tigers, cats and elephants, all together. She picked the tiger book and hugged it tight.

"Peas go with peas," she said. "Animal books go with animal books."

She found her other boot by the door on the way out. She sat down and put it on, right there on the library steps.

"Tiger time," she said.

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
knowledge_domain: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
fact: A step stool can help a small child reach the sink, with a grown-up nearby.
story:
Juliette wanted to wash her hands all by herself. But the sink was too high. Her hands could not reach the water. "Too high, too high!" she said.

Her dad brought a step stool. "Here is your step stool," he said. He stayed close by her side. Juliette climbed up. Now her hands could reach the water. "I can do it!" she said.

She put soap on her hands. She rubbed and rubbed. "Bubbles, bubbles!" she sang. She counted to twenty. It took a long, long time. The bubbles went down the drain. Her hands were clean and shiny.

"Now we can eat," said Dad. He held up a cookie. Juliette looked at her hands. "Clean hands get a party treat!" she said. Dad laughed. "A cookie party for two." Juliette rode her step stool down and ran to the table. She clapped her soapy-clean hands. "Cookie time!"

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Colors come in lighter and darker kinds, like light blue and dark blue, and both are still called blue.
story:
Lena sat at her big table. She had a pile of crayons. She wanted to draw the sky.

She found her blue crayon. But it was dark like the night sky. "I need light blue," she said.

Erica was there to play. She held up a navy crayon. "This one is blue," said Erica.

Lena shook her head. "That one is too dark. Blue is light like the sky."

They put all the blues on the table. There were five blue crayons. Lena lined them up. The palest one went first. The darkest one went last. They made a long row, light to dark.

"Look," said Erica. "They are all still called blue."

Lena smiled. She picked the lightest blue crayon. She drew a big sky shape with soft clouds. Then she drew the sea with the dark blue crayon. The sea was still blue too.

At bath time, Lena splashed the water with her hand. The water looked light blue in her little cup. The big tub looked dark blue in the shadow. "Two blues," said Lena. "One light, one dark."

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: Waiting in line means staying in your place until it is your turn.
story:
Charles went to the library with his dad. He wanted the big white book about trucks. It sat on the shelf, and Charles could see it from far away. He began to walk faster and faster. Then he ran right to the front of the line of kids. Safa and Dani were standing there, waiting for their turn.

"Charles, you went past us," said Safa. Ms. Korhonen knelt down beside him. "This is the line," she said. Charles looked behind him. So many kids, all standing one after another. He wondered, what is a line for? He went back to his spot, behind Dani. His feet stayed still. It was hard to wait. He counted the flowers on Dani's shirt, one, two, three, four.

A boy at the front got his book. Then it was Safa's turn. Then it was Dani's turn. And then it was Charles's turn. He held out his hands. Ms. Korhonen gave him the big white truck book. "My turn," said Charles, and he hugged it tight.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Grown-ups shovel snow off paths so people can walk without slipping.
story:
David woke up and saw snow. Lots of snow! "No school today," said Mom. David jumped up and down. "Snow day!"

He put on his boots and his red hat. Mom took him to the big sledding hill. His friend Kingston was there too. They sled down fast, fast, fast. Whee!

Then David tried to walk to the sled hill steps. His feet slipped. He sat down in the snow with a plop.

Mr. Cruz was shoveling a path. He pushed the snow away with his big shovel. "Try walking here," he said. David walked on the clean path. He did not slip at all!

"Can I help?" David asked. Mr. Cruz gave him a small shovel. David pushed snow off the path. The mail carrier came by and waved. "Thank you!" she said.

Then Mom called, "Time to go cook soup!" David slid down the hill one more time. He heard the sound of Kingston laughing all the way down.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
fact: Tablets are kept away from water and drinks.
story:
Parker went to the library with his dad. Mr. Janssen had a table with tablets on it. Parker wanted to draw a cat on one.

"Can I try?" Parker asked.

"Yes," said Mr. Janssen. "First we turn it on." Parker pressed the round button. The screen lit up. His tap made it wake!

He tapped the little paint app. It opened. The app was open, just like a book. One tap, one picture page. Another tap, a new color. It was like magic, but it was not magic. His finger did it.

Parker drew a big orange cat. Then Tiago sat down beside him. Tiago set his juice cup on the table. It sat right by the tablet.

"Not there," said Mr. Janssen. "Tablets stay away from water and drinks." Tiago moved his cup to the next table. Parker looked at his own cup. He moved it too. Far away.

He drew the cat a pillow to sleep on. Then it was time to go. Parker pressed the button and held it. The screen went dark. He put the tablet in the basket, flat side down.

"Bye, tablet," said Parker. "Bye, cat."

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Never put fingers or things into an electrical outlet.
story:
Anna wanted to wash her toy duck. She went to the bathroom with her dad. The water ran into the sink. Dad felt it first. "Hot," he said. "Too hot for you." He turned the tap. Now the water felt warm and nice.

Anna washed the duck. It went splash, splash. Then she saw a little box on the wall. It had small holes in it. It was near the sink, close to her elbow.

Anna pointed at it. "What is that?" she asked.

"That is an electrical outlet," said Dad. "Never put fingers or things into an electrical outlet."

Anna looked at her fingers. She kept them on the duck. Dad plugged in his razor, and it made a noisy hum. Anna heard it buzz.

Dad put a little sign over the outlet. "There," he said. "Now it is covered."

Anna washed the duck some more. Splash, splash. "All clean," she said.

"Good girl," said Dad. "You told me. You did not touch."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At a big crowded celebration, children stay close to their grown-up.
story:
Elias went to Grandma's house. Today was a big party day. There were so many people there. There were lanterns and red paper on the door.

Elias held Mama's hand at the door. Then he saw a big table of food. There were his favorite dumplings. He let go of Mama's hand. He walked toward the dumplings all by himself.

The room was full of legs and coats. Elias could not see Mama. He could not see Grandma. His tummy felt funny. He stood still and thought. At a big party, he must stay close to his grown-up. Grandma found him by the food table. She took his hand. "Stay with me, little one," she said.

Grandma walked with him past all the people. Grandpa was lighting a candle. Grandma held Elias back from the candle. "Only grown-ups touch fire," she said. Elias watched the candle from far away. It was pretty and safe.

Then they found the dumplings together. Elias ate three dumplings. Mama sat right beside him. Grandma gave him a red envelope with money inside. Elias held Mama's hand again. The party was loud and happy. "This is my favorite day," said Elias. Grandma smiled and squeezed his hand.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
fact: When you are finished, the tablet goes back in its special place.
story:
Florence was at Grandma's house. On the shelf sat a little tablet. Florence wanted to draw on it.

Grandma showed her the round button. Florence pressed it with one finger. The screen lit up. A picture appeared!

"Now the drawing part," said Grandma. Grandma tapped the blue spot. Florence tapped it too. A big white page opened. Florence picked the red crayon on the screen. She drew a red cat. She drew a sleepy sun going down.

Soon Florence got tired of drawing. She put the tablet on the soft couch. Then Grandma came in to sit down. "Wait!" said Florence. The tablet was right where Grandma would sit!

Florence picked up the tablet. "Where does it go?" she asked. Grandma pointed to the shelf. "When you are finished, the tablet goes back in its special place," said Grandma. Florence set it on the shelf. It fit just right in its spot.

Grandma sat down on the couch. Florence climbed up beside her. On the fridge hung a plastic magnet shaped like a star. Florence pointed at it. "That star can be my next picture," she said. "A red one."

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: When a grown-up reads a book aloud, they are reading the words, not just looking at the pictures.
story:
Alexander wanted the rabbit book. It had a fuzzy cover. He hugged it to his chest. He carried it to Ms. Kamau.

"Read it, please," he said. Ms. Kamau sat down on the small red chair. She opened the front cover first. Then she turned the pages one by one. She read the words out loud. "The rabbit hopped to the garden," she read. The words sat under the picture, small and black.

Then she turned to a page with only a picture. The rabbit drank milk in the sun. Alexander waited. But Ms. Kamau was quiet.

"Read this one too," said Alexander.

"There are no words on this page," she said. "There is nothing written here to read."

Alexander leaned close. He looked and looked. He touched the page with his finger. There were marks on other pages, but not here. Only the rabbit and the milk.

"Turn it," he said. Ms. Kamau turned to the next page. The words came back. She read them all the way to the back cover.

Alexander clapped. Then he opened his fuzzy book again, at the front, all by himself. He traced the little black words with one finger.

"These say rabbit," he told Lachlan. "You wait. I will learn to say them too."

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: When you close your eyes, you cannot see the things around you.
story:
Milo ran into the bright backyard. "Let's play hide and seek," said Zak. Milo put his hands over his eyes. "Now you can't see me," he said. Zak laughed. "I can still see you, Milo. Your eyes are the only thing that can't see."

Milo peeked through his fingers. Zak was right. He could see the swing, the grass and Zak's big grin. He ran and hid behind the big tree. He could feel the bark, rough on his fingers. He could smell the flowers by the fence. He could hear Zak counting. "Ready or not, here I come!" Could Zak hear his feet on the grass?

Zak found him fast. "How did you know I was here?" asked Milo. "I saw your shoes," said Zak. Milo looked down. His shoes stuck out from the tree.

They played again. This time Milo tucked his feet in. Zak walked right past him. "Where is Milo? Maybe he is a dream!" Zak called. Milo held his breath and waited, smiling in the dark behind his safe tree.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Stay where your grown-up can see you when you are out.
story:
Livia wanted to help in the kitchen. Mom was busy at the stove. "The pot is hot," Mom said. "You stay back here." Livia stood far from the hot pot. She could see Mom. Mom could see her.

"I will get the big spoon," Livia said. She ran to the far end of the pantry. It was dark back there. Livia looked out. She could not see Mom. "Mom?" she called. Mom did not answer. Livia did not like the far end. She hurried back fast. Then Mom could see her. And Livia could see Mom.

"I like it here," Livia said. Mom gave her a brush. "Brush the crumbs off the table," said Mom. Livia brushed. The crumbs went slide, slide, into her hand. "Good helper," said Mom. Livia smiled and brushed some more.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Steam from a pot or kettle is hot and can burn, so stay back.
story: Isla wanted to see the pot bubble. Her dad put the pot on the stove. Then the water began to hum. "Can I guess what is inside?" Isla asked. "Just water," said her dad. White puffs rose up from the pot. They curled like little clouds. Isla stepped closer to peek. Her dad held out his hand. "Stay back," he said. "The steam is hot. It can burn you." Isla stopped. She stood by the door, far from the stove. The steam rose higher and higher. It faded before it touched the roof. "Wow," said Isla. "It goes up so fast!" Her dad smiled. He stirred the pot with a big spoon. Isla watched the bubbles pop and roll. They were round and small. She clapped her hands. Then her dad turned off the stove. He poured pasta into a strainer. Isla helped by holding the bread bag. She pulled out two soft slices. "The steam went away," she said. Her dad nodded. "It will come back next time we cook." Isla wondered where the steam would go. "Can we watch again tomorrow?" she asked. "Yes," said her dad. "You can be my young helper. You stand right there, and you watch." Isla stood very still. The pot sat quiet and cool now. "All done," she said, and patted the counter gently.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: We say "thank you" when someone gives us something or helps us.
story:
Hazel was at Grandma's house. Grandma had a small box for her. "This is for you," said Grandma. Hazel opened it fast. Inside was a red hat with a white pompom.

Hazel put the hat on. She ran to the mirror. "Not ugly at all!" she said. She spun around and around. Then she ran outside to show Madden, her friend from next door.

Madden looked at the hat. "Grandma gave you that?" he asked. Hazel nodded. "Was it a present?" he asked. Hazel nodded again. Then she stopped. She had not said the magic word to Grandma. Her mother had taught it to her. You say it when someone gives you something. Hazel ran back inside. Grandma was washing cups at the sink. Hazel waited by the door until Grandma looked up. "Thank you for my hat," said Hazel. Grandma smiled big. She gave Hazel a hug. "You are so welcome," said Grandma. Hazel held the pompom and smiled too.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: A tag on a pet's collar tells people how to reach its family if the pet gets lost.
story:
Parker came home with a small puppy. The puppy had soft brown fur. Parker named him Buddy.

Then Buddy wiggled out the door. He ran across the yard. Parker called and called. Buddy did not come back. Parker felt like crying.

His dad said, "Let's check his collar." Buddy had a tag on his collar. His dad read the tag out loud. It said their phone number. A neighbour found Buddy down the street. She saw the tag. She called the number. Parker and his dad ran to get Buddy.

Parker hugged Buddy tight. "Your tag helped you come home," Parker said. Now Parker held Buddy's leash every day. He filled the water bowl. He gave Buddy soft pats. Parker was a proud big helper. At night, Buddy slept in his new bed. Parker whispered, "Good night, Buddy." Buddy wagged his little tail.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: In a power cut, the house gets quieter because machines like the fridge stop humming.
story:
Hailey was drawing in the backyard. It was a sunny day, but the sky was getting dark. Then the lights in the house went out. "A power cut," said Dad. "The power is off."

Hailey went to the back door. She stood very still. "It's so quiet," she said. Dad nodded. "The fridge stopped humming. The power made it go."

Hailey listened hard. She heard a bird in the tree. She heard her own breath. She heard a little tap, tap, tap. "Dad, what is that?" she asked. They listened together. "Rain," said Dad. "It's starting to rain."

Hailey put out her hand. The drops fit right in her palm. Then the rain stopped. The sun came back. Inside, the fridge began to hum again. "The power is on!" Dad called. Hailey laughed. The hum filled the house like a song. "I missed you, fridge," she said. Dad gave her a big hug.

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
fact: Holding the paper still with your other hand helps keep it from sliding.
story:
Ayla sat at the kitchen table. She had a pencil and some paper. Mom sat next to her with a towel and a cup of tea.

"Can you write your name?" Mom asked.

Ayla wanted to try. She held the pencil with her whole fist. She made a big round A. Then the paper slid away. Her line went crooked. The letter looked wobbly.

"My paper keeps moving," Ayla said.

She tried again. She pressed hard. The paper slid again. She frowned and put her head down.

Mom sat close by her side. "You can try again," Mom said softly. "Your hands can work together."

Ayla sat up. She put her left hand flat on the paper. She held the paper still. Then she drew with the pencil.

The paper did not slide. Her A stood up straight. Her Y had two neat arms. Her L had a good tall line.

"Mom, look!" said Ayla. "I did it!"

She wrote the whole name. A Y L A. All four letters, neat and small.

Mom clapped her hands. "Let's ask Dad to come and see," she said.

Dad came to the table. He looked at the paper. "That's your name!" he said. "You wrote it all by yourself."

Ayla smiled big. She turned the paper toward him. "This is me," she said.

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
knowledge_domain: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
fact: Rhyming words end with the same sound, like cat and hat.
story:
Rose sat on the little red mat. Mr. Lim tapped the drum. Tap, tap, tap. Rose clapped along with the taps. Her claps went the same speed as the drum.

"Now let's sing," said Mr. Lim. "The cat sat on the mat. The cat wore a big red..."

Amelya stopped. "I forgot the word!"

"Ask Rose," said Mehreen. "Rose knows it."

Rose thought hard. The cat wore a big red... She tried a word. "Mat?"

Amelya laughed. "A red mat on his head? That is so silly!"

"The word ends like cat," said Amelya. "Cat. Hat!"

"Hat!" said Rose. "The cat wore a big red hat!"

They sang it again. Tap, tap, tap went the drum. Clap, clap, clap went Rose. "And next he found an egg," sang Mehreen.

"A red egg?" said Rose. "You are so mean to that cat!"

Everyone giggled. Mr. Lim tapped faster. Rose clapped faster to keep up. "My hands can go fast too!" she said.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
fact: Spread butter with the flat side of the knife, pushing it across the bread.
story:
Louis stood in the kitchen. The toast was on his plate. Mom had made it warm for him. Louis wanted to butter it all by himself.

He took his knife. He poked the toast with the pointy tip. The toast tore. Little crumbs went everywhere. "Oh no," said Louis. Mom handed him a new piece of toast. "Try the flat side," she said.

Louis looked at the flat side. He pushed it across the bread. The butter came off the knife. It spread out smooth and shiny. "It works!" said Louis. He pushed again and again. Soon the toast was all covered.

Next came the milk. Louis held the cup with two hands. He poured slowly. One little drop spilled on the table. But the cup did not tip over. "I did it!" said Louis.

Mom smiled at him. Louis took a big bite of his toast. "Yummy," he said. "Can I do it again tomorrow?"

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
fact: One way to put on a coat is to lay it on the floor, put your arms in the sleeves and flip it over your head.
story:
Aiden was at Grandma's house. Snow was falling outside. He wanted to play in it fast!

Grandma gave him his red coat. Aiden pushed one arm in. Then he wiggled and wiggled. He could not find the other sleeve. The coat fell down. "Oh no!" said Aiden.

Just then his friend Amal came to the door. Amal had her coat on already. "Watch this," she said. She laid her coat on the floor. She put her arms in the sleeves. Then she flipped it over her head. The coat was on!

Aiden laid his coat on the floor. He put his arms in the sleeves. He flipped it over his head. The coat was on him! He pulled the zipper up, up, up. It went zzzzzip!

"I did it!" said Aiden. "We can go far in the snow!" said Amal. Grandma waved from the window. Aiden ran out the door into the white, white snow.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Soon means in a little while.
story:
Willow went to the park today. Yesterday it rained, so she could not come. The grass was still wet and shiny.

Willow saw the big yellow swing. She wanted to ride on it. But Ava was on it now. Willow asked, "Can I have a turn?"

"Soon," said Ava. Willow frowned. "What does soon mean?"

Ms. Nowak was sitting on a bench nearby. "Soon means in a little while," she said. Willow sat on the wood chips to wait. She counted the birds. One, two, three.

Ava pumped her legs. The swing went up and down. Then Ava jumped off. "Your turn now!" she said.

Willow ran fast. She climbed on and rode the swing. Her hair flew in the wind. She touched the sky with her toes.

Then Khadijah came by with a little carton of milk. She sat down on the wood chips. "I want a turn too," she said.

"You can have it soon," said Willow. Ava pushed the swing soft and slow. Khadijah watched the swing go up. Willow counted to three again.

Then Willow jumped down. "Now it is your turn," she said.

Khadijah clapped her hands and ran to the swing.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
fact: When pretend play is finished, the toys get put away.
story:
Harrison ran to the pretend kitchen at the playground. Belle was already there. "I am cooking soup," she said. She stirred a pot full of red and yellow leaves. Harrison picked up a tiny cup. He poured pretend tea. The cup felt bumpy in his hands. The leaves smelled like dirt and rain.

Then it was time to go home. Ms. Wanjiru rang the bell. Harrison started to run. But Belle stopped. She put the leaves back in the pot. She set the cups in the middle of the little shelf. "We have to clean up," she said. "When pretend play is finished, the toys get put away." Harrison looked at the messy kitchen. So that was the rule!

Harrison picked up the spoon. He put it in the pot. He set the little plates in a neat row. The kitchen looked new again. Would Ms. Wanjiru see it? She smiled and clapped her hands. "What a tidy kitchen," she said. Harrison hugged his pretend pot. "Bye bye, kitchen," he whispered. "See you tomorrow."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In games like soccer and basketball, the team with more points at the end wins.
story:
Lennon sat at the big table. Her fries were hot and salty. Lisa sat next to her. Penelope sat across. On the wall was a huge screen. A soccer game was on.

"Look at the blue team run!" said Lennon. "They run so fast. They run the most."

The blue team ran and ran. But the ball went in the other net. The red team jumped up high.

Lennon frowned. She pointed at the screen. "Wait. The red team did not run much."

"That is the score," said Lisa. She pointed to the numbers.

Lennon looked. Red had two goals. Blue had zero. The wind blew a plastic napkin off the table and Lennon caught it, giggling.

Then red scored one more. The whistle blew. The game was over.

"Red wins!" said Penelope. "They have more points at the end!"

Lennon clapped her salty hands. "So running fast is not the game. Points are the game!"

She ate another fry and waved at the screen. "Goodbye, blue team. Practice your kicks!"

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Wet and dry are opposites.
story:
Elias ran out to the school yard. It had rained all morning. Now the sun made the puddles shine like little blue mirrors. A big puddle sat by the gate. A small puddle sat by the wall. Elias stomped right into the big one. Splash! Cold water went into his shoe. His sock was wet. Very wet.

"Wet and dry are opposites," said Mr. Grant. "Come with me." Elias walked slow through the hall. Squish, squish, squish. Mr. Grant found a dry pair of socks in the big box. Elias pulled off the wet sock. He blew on his cold toes to warm them up. Then he put on the dry sock. It felt soft and warm. Then came a surprise. The lamp on the shelf blinked on. The lamp had a plug on a timer, and it buzzed a little. "What made the lamp go on?" Elias asked. Mr. Grant smiled. "Something inside," he said. Elias sat under the warm lamp until his other shoe dried.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
fact: Stopping before the cup is full to the top makes it easier to carry without spilling.
story:
Mackenzie woke up in the tent. "Toast time!" she shouted. At the campsite table, her dad set down warm bread. Mackenzie took the butter knife. She spread and spread. The butter got stuck in one lump. She tried again, slow and small. One, two, three little strokes. Now the butter covered the whole slice!

Next came the milk. Mackenzie wanted to pour it all by herself. She tipped the cup high. Milk went glug, glug, glug, right up to the very top. She grabbed the cup with both hands. She took one step. The milk wobbled. Then the milk spilled all over the table. "Oh no," said Mackenzie.

She got a towel and wiped it up. Then she tried again. This time she poured and stopped before the cup was full to the top. She left some room. Mackenzie picked up the cup. One step, two steps, three steps. The milk stayed in! "I did it!" she said. Kaysen clapped from his seat. Mackenzie took a big drink and smiled. "More milk, please," she said.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: A clock shows what time it is.
story:
Theo went to the store with Dad. Today they needed apples and bread. Yesterday the bread was all gone. Tomorrow they would have toast.

Theo wanted to roll the cart. "Can I push it now?" he asked. "Later," said Dad. "First we get the apples." Theo looked up. There was a big clock on the wall. It had hands and numbers.

"When is later?" Theo asked. Dad pointed at the clock. "The clock shows what time it is," he said. "When the big hand moves to the top, we will go home." Theo watched the hand. It ticked and ticked. Then it reached the top. "Now it is time!" he said. Dad smiled. "Yes. You watched the clock with your own eye." They rolled the cart to the door. "Can we come back tomorrow?" Theo asked. "Tomorrow," said Dad, "we will get jam."

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: People wear hats, mittens, boots and warm coats to play in the snow.
story:
Grayson woke up and looked out the window. The snow was loud on the glass. "Mom, come see!" he called.

It was a snow day. No school today. Grayson wanted to build a snowman. He ran to the door in his pajamas. He opened it fast. The cold air came in. His fingers got cold right away. "Brrr," said Grayson. He ran back inside.

Mom helped him get dressed. He put on warm boots. He put on a big warm coat. Mom found his hat. "Where are your mittens?" she asked. Grayson looked and looked. He could not find them. He almost forgot all about his snowman.

There they were, under the chicken puzzle. Grayson pulled them out. "My mittens!" he said. Mom helped him put them on.

Grayson went outside. His boots went crunch, crunch. His fingers were warm in the mittens. He patted snow onto a big ball. He patted more and more. Soon his snowman stood up tall.

Grayson put his hat on the snowman's head. The snowman wore a hat, just like him. "Goodbye, snowman," said Grayson. He waved his mitten hand all the way to the door.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
fact: On a snowy day, mittens or gloves keep your hands warm.
story:
Aria looked out the window. The sky was white and the snow fell down. "It is a snowy day," said Aria. She put on her boots. She put on her red coat. She ran outside to play.

The snow was soft and bumpy in spots. Aria made a snowball with her bare hands. The snowball was round like a triangle was not. She laughed and threw it at a post.

Then her hands felt cold. Very cold. Her fingers hurt a little. Aria ran back inside. "My hands are cold," she said. Her mom got her mittens. They were blue with white stars.

Aria put the mittens on. She went back out. She made another snowball. Her hands stayed warm this time. The wind blew, but her mittens kept her hands cozy. Aria made one snowball, then two, then three. "Snowball mountain," she said. She stacked them up tall. Then she gave the top one a little nose made of snow. "Hello, snow friend," said Aria.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
fact: Pockets in a coat can hold small things like mittens.
story:
Zayn stood in the garage with his dad. It was cold outside. Snow was on the ground near the big door.

Zayn had a new coat. He wanted to put it on all by himself. He pushed his arms in. One arm went in. The other arm went in too. Now for the zipper. He pulled it up, up, up. It stuck halfway. His dad waited quietly. Zayn pulled again. Zip! It went all the way to the top.

"I did it!" said Zayn.

Then he saw his mittens on the floor. He had dropped one. He picked it up. Where could it go? He found a little pocket on his coat. He tucked both mittens inside. The pocket held them tight.

"Ready to meet Beckett at the lake?" his dad asked.

"Yes!" said Zayn. He patted his furry mittens in the pocket. Then he held his dad's hand and walked out into the snow.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
fact: A strong wind can blow a hat right off your head.
story:
Zachary stood at the front door. He put on his red hat. The trees outside were bending. The leaves flew all around. "It is windy," said his mom. Zachary stepped outside. The wind pushed his hair. Then the wind blew his hat right off his head.

The hat rolled across the grass. Zachary ran after it. "Come back, hat!" he called. His friend Danika was walking by. "I will help you," she said. She ran too. The hat flew high. Then it landed in a bush. Zachary grabbed it. He held it tight.

He ran back to the door. His dad gave him a clip. The clip held the hat to his coat. Zachary jumped in the wind again. The hat stayed on his head. He laughed. Zachary felt tired from running. "That was fun," said Danika. Zachary smiled and waved. "See you tomorrow!"
